meaning: A resource a program can run out of, such as a core's arithmetic, memory bandwidth or memory latency; the part a program runs out of first sets its speed.
A program run in place of the arm's real workload, useful as far as it runs out of the same part of the machine.
The physics engine that steps the simulated scenes of this dive; one step advances a scene by one timestep.
The set of event counters inside a processor core, such as cycles, stalled slots and retired micro-operations.
The record of one program on one core: its rate, its four slot shares and its memory stall.
The Linux tool that reads the PMU counters around one run of a program.
A lower internal precision for float32 matrix multiplies on NVIDIA GPUs, with a float32 result; PyTorch allows it through torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high").
What perf does when a core has too few counters for the requested events: each event counts for part of the run and its total is scaled up, which costs accuracy in ratios of two events.
A method that finds a core's bottleneck from its event counters by sorting every slot into one of four shares: retiring, front-end bound, back-end bound and bad speculation.
A fetch into the core's second-level cache from further out in the memory system; refills per thousand instructions show how hard a program leans on memory.
Arm's finer counters that split a first-level share, for example back-end stalls into core causes and memory causes; not counted in these runs.
The name under which Linux exposes one core type's PMU, such as armv8_pmuv3_1 for the Cortex-X925 on a DGX Spark; perf events are named through it.
The Linux command that pins a program to chosen cores, so its counters come from one known core type.
A small loop built to load one part of a core, such as its multiply-add units or its memory.
One chance per clock cycle for a core to start one micro-operation; a core has a fixed number per cycle.
One of the small steps a core splits an instruction into; slots start them and the back end executes them.
A core's slots per cycle: 10 on the Cortex-X925, 5 on the Cortex-A725, 6 (derived) on the Cortex-A78AE.
The share of slots that started work the program kept.
A core predicting which way a branch goes and starting the instructions beyond it before the branch is resolved.
Throwing away the work a core started on a wrong prediction and restarting on the right path.
The share of slots spent on work thrown away after a wrong prediction, and on the restart after it.
The share of slots left empty because the half of the core that fetches and decodes instructions had nothing ready.
The share of slots left empty because the half of the core that executes instructions could take no more.
The share of cycles the back end spent waiting for data from memory, read from a separate counter in a second execution.
Finished instructions divided by clock cycles; with the clock and the instructions per unit of work it sets a core's throughput.
Arm's adjustment that moves the cycles a core spends recovering from a flush from front-end bound to bad speculation.
The event and formula definitions Arm publishes for each core, including its top-down formulas and slots per cycle; there is no file for the Cortex-A78AE.
The bytes per second that memory can stream to a core.
The time one isolated read from memory takes.
One instruction that computes a x b + c; a loop of independent scalar ones measures a core's multiply-add throughput, with the vector units left out.
A loop that streams through arrays larger than the caches, used to measure memory bandwidth.
A loop in which each read gives the address of the next, used to measure memory latency.
The core's cache of address translations; a pointer chase over a large area also pays its misses.
Arm's vector instructions, which work on several numbers at once.
The function that sets negative values to zero, applied after a layer of a neural network.
The interface MuJoCo uses for hardware-accelerated rendering with no display.
A renderer that draws triangles onto pixels, as MuJoCo's built-in renderers do, with no ray tracing.
One function launched on the GPU.
NVIDIA's profiler for a single GPU kernel; it reports compute and memory throughput as shares of the GPU's maximum.
One of the GPU's processing units, repeated many times across the chip.
The GPU's general execution path, as opposed to its tensor cores.
The GPU units built for the matrix arithmetic of neural networks.
The median time per call and the time only one call in a hundred exceeds.
AWS's own Arm processors; their cores are Arm Neoverse designs.
The imitation-learning policy of section 4 that predicts a chunk of future actions.
A small vision-language-action model, the policy family of section 5.
The latent world model of section 7.
NVIDIA's GPU telemetry tool, which samples activity of the GPU's parts over time.
The Jetson's built-in monitor, which reports processor, GPU, memory and power readings, including the GPU clock.
NVIDIA's timeline profiler, which shows when the GPU works and when it waits.
